newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-NZ markets unmoved by Peters' budget paper.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-NZ markets unmoved by Peters' budget paper.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters, in his first major set-piece statement since taking the portfolio in December, failed to impress economists on Tuesday when he spelled out the government's spending plans over the next three years.
The Budget Policy Statement, a precursor to June's Budget, outlined slightly lower new spending in 1997/98 than previously signalled, but higher spending in 1999/00.
Peters said persistent inflation pressures meant a fiscal easing was not appropriate, and the new government would stick within its self-imposed spending limits.
"Now is not the time for a fiscal easing, which might increase the imbalance between domestic strength and external pressure," he told journalists.
Financial markets and economists were largely unimpressed.
"I'm not sure what he means there, because he has just gone out and eased fiscal policy massively over the next three years," Bankers Trust NZ Chief Economist David Plank told Reuters Financial TV.
"I suppose what he meant is that there is no room for fiscal easing over and above the very large fiscal easing we have already done. I hope he doesn't believe he is being fiscally tight."
Peters said fresh spending in the first year of the centre-right government's three year term would be NZ$250 million lower than the $1.2 billion originally planned.
But he still plans to spend an extra $5 billion above what the former conservative National Party government planned.
The projections in Tuesday's statement show surpluses that are still healthy, but substantially smaller than previous forecasts.
A budget surplus of NZ$3.3 billion, 3.2 percent of GDP, is predicted for 1997/98, against $3.1 billion previously forecast.

The 1999/00 surplus forecast has fallen to $3.5 billion from $6.1 billion. This could fall a further $1 billion if planned tax cuts proceed; the cuts were not included in the forecasts because they are conditional on a referendum on compulsory pensions due in September.

"The surplus in 1999/00 is a little exaggerated because they have removed $1 billion of tax cuts that were in the previous document," National Bank of New Zealand Chief Economist Adrian Orr told Reuters Financial TV.
"It's still positive... but it is putting a lot more pressure on inflation and interest rates than what our Treasurer is prepared to confess," he said.

Asked how prudent Peters was being, Orr said: "It's classic Winston Peters. There are lots of good words there but then his actions are wholly different so the markets will remain as cautious as ever if this is his degree of fiscal prudence."

Indicator 90-day bank bills rose around six basis points to 7.72 percent after the statement. Those higher rates helped support the Kiwi dollar which was already near a historically high rate of 70.2 U.S. cents. The share market largely ignored the document, remaining in slightly positive territory.
BT's Plank said that what worried him was the extra spending planned in the coalition's third year in power.
"What they have done is they have ended up spending less in Year One and more in Year Three and that increase in Year Three is permanent.
"So they have actually gone out and permanently worsened the fiscal position by the end of the period over and above what it was in the Coalition Document," Plank said.

Plank predicts key economic forecasts due to be published by the Reserve Bank next week will see the central bank sustantially revise up the inflation track in 1998 because of the extra spending. The inflation target band has been widened to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent.
